title: North Sikkim on a budget: where the money goes
meta_description: How to see Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen and Dzongu for less: group packages, shared jeeps to Mangan, cheap months, and the extras that are not worth paying for.
summary: A careful traveller can see Lachung and Yumthang for about ₹8,000–10,000 per person from Siliguri, and both valleys for about ₹11,000–14,000, indicative 2026. The savings come from a shared group package for the permit zone, shared jeeps everywhere else, family hotels, shoulder months and saying no to most extras.

sections.heading: Where the money actually goes
paras: North Sikkim is not cheap in the way a Darjeeling homestay is cheap, because the rules force you to spend on one thing: a registered local vehicle. Tourists cannot self-drive or ride shared jeeps beyond the permit checkposts. Every trip to Lachung, Yumthang, Lachen or Gurudongmar goes in a car or jeep booked through a registered Sikkim tour operator, who also files your permit. That vehicle is usually half the bill, and how many people share it decides whether your trip is expensive or not.

Hotels, food and permits are a smaller share. Lachung and Lachen family hotels are simple, and most packages include breakfast and dinner because there is little else to eat in the evening. Here is what three nights and four days from Siliguri, Gangtok to Lachung and back, looks like per person, sharing a room. These are indicative 2026 ranges; May, Puja week and New Year cost more.

sections.heading: Group seat or private car
paras: The single biggest saving is a shared group package from Gangtok. Operators fill a Bolero, Xylo or similar vehicle with eight to ten travellers, put everyone in the same family hotel and sell the trip as one price that covers the permit, the seat, the room and most meals. In 2026 a one-night Lachung trip costs about ₹3,500–5,500 per person and a two-night Lachen and Lachung loop about ₹6,000–9,000. A private car for the same loop costs about ₹16,000–22,000 per vehicle before hotels.

The trade-offs are real: you leave when the group leaves, you sit where you are put, and the hotel is chosen for you. For students, solo travellers and couples who do not mind that, it is the honest cheap option. For a family of four or five, a private car often costs about the same per head as four or five group seats, with far more freedom. Our separate guide on group tours and private cars works through the numbers.

sections.heading: Getting up the hill for less
paras: From Siliguri, shared jeeps and SNT buses run to Gangtok through the morning; a jeep seat costs about ₹350–500 and takes 4–5 hours on NH10 along the Teesta. Go before 1 pm, when departures thin out. From Gangtok, shared jeeps leave the North Sikkim stand for Mangan, about 65 km and 3 hours, for ₹250–350 a seat, indicative 2026. That road is open to Indians without a Protected Area Permit as far as the Toong checkpost.

This matters for budget travellers heading to Dzongu or Singhik, because homestays and the Singhik lodge are reached from Mangan, and a ₹300 jeep seat replaces a ₹4,000 car. Coming back, you can take the shorter road from Mangan down through Dikchu and Singtam to NH10 instead of returning via Gangtok. Shared fares move with fuel prices, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Sleeping and eating cheaply
paras: In Lachung and Lachen, group packages use family hotels with simple rooms, blankets and a shared dining room. They are fine for one night if you check three things: hot water in the morning, heating in winter, and whether the heater is charged extra. A homestay such as Bichu Homestay in Lachung costs about ₹2,000–3,500 a room night with breakfast and dinner, indicative 2026, and gives you better food for the money than many hotels.

Food beyond the hotel is limited. Tea at Thangu or Yumthang stalls costs ₹30–60 a cup and a plate of noodles or momos ₹80–200. Buy dry snacks, fruit and chocolate in Gangtok's Lal Bazaar before you go, because the same things cost more higher up. Carry a refillable bottle: packaged water is banned in Lachen and above by the village council, and Sikkim discourages it statewide.
Carry enough cash for the whole north. ATMs above Mangan are few and often empty, and card machines in Lachung and Lachen are unreliable. Keep small notes for tea, boot hire and toilets.

sections.heading: The permit-free north
paras: Some of the best North Sikkim days cost almost nothing and need no Protected Area Permit for Indian citizens. The open stretch of the North Sikkim Highway runs from Gangtok to just beyond Mangan, and shared jeeps go the whole way. If your permit is delayed or the road above Chungthang is shut, these places save the trip.
list: Kabi Lungchok, about 20 km from Gangtok: stone pillars where, by Sikkimese tradition, the Lepcha sage Thekong Tek and the Bhutia prince Khye Bumsa swore blood brotherhood. Free.
Phodong Monastery, 38 km from Gangtok: an 18th-century Karma Kagyu gompa, one of the six main monasteries of Sikkim, with a masked chaam in December. Free; an offering is welcome.
Mangan bazaar: the headquarters town of the district, where 100 g of local large cardamom costs about ₹150–300.
Singhik, 4 km beyond Mangan: a ridge at about 1,560 m facing Kanchenjunga and Siniolchu. The government Singhik Bungalow costs about ₹2,000–3,500 a room night, indicative 2026.
Dzongu, across the Teesta from Mangan: the Lepcha reserve, which needs its own permit through your homestay, with all meals included at about ₹2,000–3,500 per person a night.

sections.heading: What to skip and what to pay for
paras: Zero Point is the classic upsell. It costs about ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle, indicative 2026, climbs to about 4,660 m, roughly 2,000 m above Lachung in one morning, and is often closed. Pay for it on the morning itself, only if the sky is clear, the road is open and everyone feels well. Never pay for it in advance as part of a package.

Snow gear is the second. Boots and padded jackets hire in Lachung for ₹150–300 an item. Between April and November you rarely need them at Yumthang if you bring a warm jacket and good shoes. Oxygen cans bought in Gangtok cost ₹500–900 and offer brief relief at best; they are not a treatment. Yak rides and photo stops are optional.

Pay properly for two things. One is a warm room in winter, because a cold night ruins the next day. The other is a buffer day at the end of the trip, because a landslide that makes you miss a flight costs far more than one extra night in Gangtok.

sections.heading: When to go for the lowest prices
paras: North Sikkim rates follow Indian school holidays. Late April, May, the Durga Puja to Diwali weeks and Christmas to New Year are the dearest. The cheapest workable months are January and February outside New Year, the first half of March, and the second half of November. Winter is cold but dry and roads to Lachung usually stay open; November is clear and quiet after Diwali.

June to August is cheapest of all but not worth it: landslides close roads and permits are often suspended for weeks, as in 2025. September is the reopening month, and operators discount to restart the season; aim for its last ten days. Since the October 2023 flood, closures can come in any month, so take refundable bookings and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to visit North Sikkim
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep from Siliguri to Gangtok for about ₹350–500, then join a shared group package from Gangtok that includes the permit, a vehicle seat, a family hotel and most meals. In 2026 a one-night Lachung package costs about ₹3,500–5,500 per person and a two-night Lachen and Lachung loop about ₹6,000–9,000, indicative. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a 3-night Lachung trip cost from Siliguri
faqs.a: About ₹8,000–10,000 per person twin sharing on a frugal plan, indicative 2026: shared jeeps to Gangtok, two budget Gangtok nights and a one-night Lachung group package. With a private car and comfortable hotels, expect about ₹18,000–25,000 per person. May, Puja week and New Year cost more.

faqs.q: Can I go to Lachung by shared jeep
faqs.a: No. Shared jeeps run only as far as the permit checkposts, around Mangan. Beyond that, tourists must travel in a registered local vehicle booked through a registered Sikkim operator, who files the Protected Area Permit. A seat in a shared group package is the closest thing to a shared jeep and the cheapest way to reach Lachung.

faqs.q: Is a North Sikkim group package good value
faqs.a: For solo travellers, students and couples, yes. It bundles the permit, a vehicle seat, a family hotel and breakfast and dinner at about a third of the cost of a private car. You give up control of timing, seating and hotel choice. Read what is included: Zero Point, lunches and heaters are usually extra.

faqs.q: Is Zero Point worth the extra money
faqs.a: Only on a clear morning when everyone feels well. It costs about ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle, indicative 2026, so it is cheaper per head in a full car. It is often closed after snow and from about mid-December. Decide on the morning and never prepay it in a package. Yumthang alone is a full and rewarding outing.

faqs.q: Which month is cheapest for North Sikkim
faqs.a: July and August are cheapest but roads and permits are unreliable. For low prices with a working trip, choose January and February outside New Year, early March or late November. Hotels discount, group seats are easy to find and roads to Lachung are usually open, though snow can close them for a day or two in winter.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in North Sikkim
faqs.a: Yes. Carry enough cash from Gangtok or Mangan for the whole trip above Mangan. ATMs further north are few and often out of service, and card machines in Lachung and Lachen hotels and shops do not always work. Keep small notes for tea, boot hire, toilets and Zero Point, which is paid locally.

faqs.q: Can I visit Mangan and Singhik without a permit
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no Protected Area Permit for Kabi Lungchok, Phodong, Mangan and Singhik, which lie on the open stretch of the North Sikkim Highway. Shared jeeps run from Gangtok to Mangan for ₹250–350 a seat. Foreign nationals need their Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Dzongu, across the river, needs its own permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How can a family save on North Sikkim
faqs.a: Book one private car for a family of four or five instead of separate group seats; the vehicle costs the same for two or five, so per head it is close to the group price with far more freedom. Travel in shoulder weeks, hire snow gear rather than buying it, skip Zero Point unless the day is perfect and keep a buffer night rather than risk a missed flight.
